title: Checkpoint 6 Science — Practice Test 1
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Practice test
summary: A full timed Checkpoint-style Science test — two 35-minute papers worth 40 marks each — set in a school garden, on the Red Sea coast and on a fossil hunt in the Western Desert, with automatic marking, a mark scheme and full worked solutions.

items: This is a full practice test in the style of the **Cambridge Primary Checkpoint Science (0097)** test taken at the end of Stage 6. It covers the whole Stage 6 curriculum: biology, chemistry, physics, Earth and space, and thinking and working scientifically.
There are **two papers**. Each paper lasts **35 minutes** and is worth **40 marks** (80 marks in total). The timer starts when you press Start.

**Calculator:** the cover of the real Paper 1 says "You may use a calculator", so a calculator is allowed in Paper 1. For Paper 2, follow what your teacher or the paper says — the calculations in this test are simple enough to do by hand.

**Equipment:** a black or dark blue pen, an HB pencil for diagrams and graphs, and a calculator. In the real test you write your answers and working on the question paper, and no additional materials are needed.
You can **write your answers on paper first** if you like — download the question paper (PDF) and do the test the real way, then type your answers in or mark them with the mark scheme (PDF).

**How marking works here:** typed answers (numbers, short words and multiple choice) are checked automatically. Written answers (explanations, descriptions) you mark yourself at the end: compare your answer with the mark scheme and give yourself the marks you have really earned.
Look at the marks for each part: **[2] means two separate points**. Give units (g, N, °C, s) with your numbers.
Your score is a **practice score** to show you what to revise. It is **not** an official Cambridge result.

questions.q: (b) How many food chains in this food web include the sparrow?
questions.e:
Follow every path that passes through the sparrow:
1. cabbage → caterpillar → sparrow → cat
2. cabbage → aphid → ladybird → sparrow → cat
3. grass → grasshopper → sparrow → cat
So **3** food chains. (The fourth chain, grass → grasshopper → lizard → cat, does not include the sparrow.)
Tip: always write the chains out — it is easy to miss one.

questions.q:
(d) The gardener sprays the cabbages with a pesticide to kill the aphids. The pesticide is toxic and it stays in animals' bodies.
Explain why the cat could be harmed, even though it never eats cabbage.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the pesticide/toxin passes along the food chain, e.g. aphid → ladybird → sparrow → cat (accept: animals that ate the cabbage/aphids are eaten by animals higher up the chain). 1 mark: each animal eats many of the animals below it, so the amount of toxin builds up / the cat collects a large amount of toxin. Do not accept: 'the cat eats the pesticide' with no food chain idea.
questions.e: The aphids (and caterpillars) take in the pesticide when they eat the cabbage. Ladybirds eat many aphids, sparrows eat many ladybirds and caterpillars, and the cat eats sparrows. The toxin **moves along the food chain** and, because each animal eats many of the ones below it, the amount **builds up** — so the cat can get a harmful amount without ever touching a cabbage.

questions.e: The club **changes** the amount of compost (0, 2, 4, 6 spoonfuls), so that is the independent variable. The height is what they measure (dependent variable). The type of soil is kept the same (sandy) — a control variable.

questions.q: (f) Use your science to explain why adding compost helps plants to grow in sandy soil.
questions.ms: 1 mark for one of: compost is organic matter that adds nutrients/minerals to the soil; OR compost holds water so the sandy soil does not dry out as quickly (sandy soil drains quickly). Do not accept: 'compost is food for plants' without nutrients/minerals.

questions.ms: 1 mark each for any two different ways: put a lid on the barrel / cover or empty still water (so mosquitoes cannot breed); use insect repellent (on skin); wear long sleeves and long trousers / cover the skin; use mosquito nets or screens; avoid the garden at dawn/dusk when mosquitoes bite most. Do not accept: 'wash hands' / 'take medicine' / two answers that are the same idea.
questions.e: For example: **(1) put a lid on the water barrel (or empty it) so mosquitoes cannot lay eggs there**; **(2) wear long sleeves and trousers or put on insect repellent**. Other good answers: use nets or screens, avoid the garden at dusk.

questions.q: (b) The pupils pick tomatoes from the garden to eat. Explain why they should wash their hands and the tomatoes first.

questions.e: Soil and dirty hands can carry **pathogens (germs such as bacteria or parasite eggs)**. Washing removes them, so they are not swallowed with the food and cannot cause disease.

questions.q: (c) Mariam scratches her arm on a rose thorn and it bleeds. Which of the body's defences against pathogens has been broken?
questions.e: The **skin** is a barrier that stops pathogens getting into the body. A cut makes a gap in it, so the cut should be cleaned and covered. Mucus traps pathogens in the nose and airways; stomach acid kills pathogens in swallowed food.

questions.q: (e) Explain why the lamps in circuit Z are brighter than the lamps in circuit Y.
questions.ms: 1 mark: in Z (parallel) each lamp is connected directly to the cells / has its own path (loop) to the cells / gets the full push of the cells, but in Y (series) the lamps share the push of the cells / the current must go through both lamps. Accept: 'in Y the energy is shared between two lamps'.
questions.e: In the parallel circuit Z, **each lamp has its own path to the cells**, so each lamp gets the full push of the two cells. In the series circuit Y, the two lamps **share** the push of the cells, so each one is dimmer.

questions.q: (c) A space robot takes the same fossil to the Moon, where gravity is weaker. Which statement is correct?
c: Its mass and its weight both stay the same.
Its mass and its weight are both less.
Its mass stays the same but its weight is less.
Its mass is less but its weight stays the same.
questions.e: **Mass** is the amount of matter in the fossil — that does not change when it moves. **Weight** is the pull of gravity on it, so weaker gravity on the Moon means a smaller weight. Answer C.

questions.q: (d) Gravity on the Moon is 1.6 N/kg. Calculate the weight of the fossil on the Moon.
questions.e:
Weight = mass (in kg) × gravity = 0.25 kg × 1.6 N/kg = **0.4 N**.
Common mistake: using 250 (grams) instead of 0.25 kg, giving 400.

questions.q: (a) Which rock is igneous? Write J, K or L.
questions.e: **K**. Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and solidifies, so it is made of **interlocking crystals** in no particular pattern, with no layers and no fossils.
questions.p:

Rock | What it looks like

K | interlocking crystals of different colours; no layers; very hard
L | crystals lined up in wavy bands; no fossils; very hard

questions.q: (b) What type of rock is L?
questions.e: **Metamorphic**. Heat and pressure deep underground change a rock without melting it; the crystals line up in bands, and any fossils are destroyed.

questions.q: (c) Rock J is a sedimentary rock. Describe how the shell fossil in rock J was formed.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a sea animal died and its shell sank to the sea floor and was (quickly) covered by sediment (sand/mud). 1 mark: more layers of sediment built up on top and squeezed/pressed the layers into rock; the shell was replaced by minerals / turned to stone (accept: left its shape/print in the rock). Marks are independent.
questions.e:
1. A sea animal died and its shell sank to the **sea floor**, where it was quickly **buried by sediment** (sand and mud).
2. Over a very long time, **more layers** of sediment built up on top. Their weight **squeezed the layers into rock**, and **minerals** slowly replaced the shell, so it became a fossil in stone.

questions.q: (d) Hana wants a quick test to help tell rock J from rock K. Which test is best?
c: Measure the temperature of each rock.
Weigh each rock on a balance.
Look at the colour of each rock.
Drip water onto each rock and see if it soaks in.
questions.e: Sedimentary rock J has small gaps between its grains, so water **soaks in**. Igneous rock K has tightly interlocking crystals, so water stays on the surface. Temperature, mass and colour do not depend on the rock type, so they cannot tell the rocks apart. Answer D.

questions.q: (a) What are the reactants in this reaction?
questions.e: **Reactants** are the substances you start with, written on the left of the arrow: rock J (the limestone in it) and vinegar. Carbon dioxide is a **product** — a new substance that is made.
questions.p:
Question 9
At school, Hana drips vinegar onto a piece of rock J. The vinegar fizzes and bubbles of carbon dioxide gas are given off.
Rock J + vinegar → new substances, including carbon dioxide

questions.q: (b) Give the evidence that shows a chemical reaction happened.
questions.e: **Bubbles of gas (fizzing)** — a gas being produced is evidence that a new substance has been made, so a chemical reaction has happened.
questions.p:

questions.q: (c) By how many degrees did the temperature change?
questions.e: Change = 21 − 13 = **8 °C** (the temperature went down). A change in temperature is evidence of a chemical reaction.
questions.p:

The science club mixes citric acid powder and bicarbonate of soda in a cup of water. They measure the temperature before and after.
Before: 21 °C | After: 13 °C

questions.q: (d) Which observation is **not** evidence of a chemical reaction?
c: The colour changes from blue to green.
Bubbles of a gas are given off.
Sugar disappears when it is stirred into water.
questions.e: When sugar dissolves no new substance is made — the sugar is still there, spread out in the water (you can taste it, and get it back by evaporating the water). Dissolving is a **reversible physical change**, so D is not evidence of a chemical reaction. Colour change, a gas being produced and a temperature change are the three kinds of evidence.
questions.p: Question 9 (continued)

questions.q: (e) Which statement is correct?

Dolphins have lungs and breathe air, like humans.
Dolphins do not need oxygen because they live in water.

questions.e: Dolphins are mammals (vertebrates) with a respiratory system like ours: they have **lungs** and must come to the surface to breathe **air**. Fish are the vertebrates that use gills. Answer B.

c: It starts at exactly the same age for everyone.
It is the time when a child's body changes into an adult's body.
It stops the body from growing taller.
questions.e: **Puberty** is the stage when the body changes from a child's body into an adult's body. It starts at different ages for different people (usually earlier in girls), happens to both boys and girls, and includes a growth spurt. Answer C.

questions.q: (b) What is the angle of reflection?
questions.e:
The angle of incidence (between the incident ray and the normal) is 30°. The angle of reflection is always equal to the angle of incidence, so it is **30°**.
Common mistake: measuring from the mirror and giving 60°.

On the beach, Laila puts a plastic bottle with its lid on into the sea water. She adds sand to the bottle, 100 g at a time, and measures how deep the bottle sits in the water.
Sand added (g) | How deep the bottle sits (cm) | Floats or sinks?
0 | 2 | floats
100 | 5 | floats
200 | 8 | floats
300 | — | sinks

questions.q: (b) Why does the bottle sink when 300 g of sand is added?
c: The water pushes up harder than before.
The sand makes the water less salty.
Its weight is now greater than the upthrust from the water.
questions.e: Adding sand increases the **mass (and so the weight)** of the bottle. At first it floats lower and the upthrust grows to balance it. With 300 g the weight becomes **greater than the biggest upthrust** the water can give, so it sinks. Answer D.

questions.q: (c) Laila wants to find out more exactly what mass of sand makes the bottle sink. Suggest how she should change her method.
questions.ms: 1 mark: add smaller amounts of sand (e.g. 10 g or 20 g at a time) between 200 g and 300 g / start from 200 g and add sand in small steps. Do not accept: 'repeat the test' alone / 'use a bigger bottle'.
questions.e: Start with 200 g of sand and **add sand in much smaller steps**, for example 10 g at a time, until the bottle sinks. This finds the sinking mass between 200 g and 300 g more exactly.

questions.q: (a) What type of scientific enquiry is this?
questions.e: The club **changes one variable** (temperature), **measures one variable** (time) and keeps the others the same (one cube, 100 ml, same stirring). That is a **fair test**. Answer B.
questions.p:
Question 6
The science club investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve. Each time they use one sugar cube and 100 ml of water, and they stir at the same speed. They plot their results on a graph.

questions.q: (b) What is the dependent variable in this investigation? (the variable they measure)
questions.ms: 1 mark: the time (taken) for the sugar (cube) to dissolve. Do not accept: 'the sugar' / 'the temperature' / 'how fast it melts'.
questions.e: The **time taken for the sugar cube to dissolve** — this is what the club measures each time.
questions.p:
Question 6
The science club investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve. Each time they use one sugar cube and 100 ml of water, and they stir at the same speed. They plot their results on a graph.

questions.q: (c) Use the graph. How long did the sugar cube take to dissolve in water at 30 °C?
questions.e: Go up from 30 °C on the temperature axis to the plotted cross, then across to the time axis: **90 s**.
questions.p:
Question 6
The science club investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve. Each time they use one sugar cube and 100 ml of water, and they stir at the same speed. They plot their results on a graph.

questions.q: (d) The club did not test water at 50 °C. Use the line on the graph to estimate how long the sugar cube would take to dissolve at 50 °C.
questions.e:
Go up from 50 °C to the curved line, then across to the time axis. The line is just below the 50 s grid line: about **49 s** (any answer from 46 s to 52 s is accepted).
Common mistake: drawing a straight line between the points at 40 °C and 60 °C and reading 51 s is close, but always read from the line that is drawn.
questions.p:
Question 6
The science club investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve. Each time they use one sugar cube and 100 ml of water, and they stir at the same speed. They plot their results on a graph.

questions.q: (e) Describe the pattern in the results.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the higher the temperature (of the water), the shorter the time to dissolve / the faster the sugar dissolves / ora. Accept: the time goes down as temperature goes up. Do not accept: 'temperature changes the time'.
questions.e: **As the temperature of the water increases, the time for the sugar to dissolve decreases** — the sugar dissolves faster in hotter water (the time drops quickly at first, then more slowly).
questions.p:
Question 6
The science club investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve. Each time they use one sugar cube and 100 ml of water, and they stir at the same speed. They plot their results on a graph.

questions.q: (f) Use the particle model to explain why sugar dissolves faster in hot water.
questions.ms: 1 mark: (in hot water) the water particles move faster / have more energy. 1 mark: so they hit the sugar particles more often/harder AND the sugar particles break away / spread out between the water particles more quickly. Do not accept: 'the sugar melts' / 'the particles get bigger'.
questions.e: In hot water the **water particles move faster** (they have more energy). They **hit the sugar particles more often and harder**, so the sugar particles break away from the cube and **spread out between the water particles** more quickly.
questions.p:
Question 6
The science club investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve. Each time they use one sugar cube and 100 ml of water, and they stir at the same speed. They plot their results on a graph.

questions.q: (a) Explain why getting salt back from sea water shows that dissolving is a reversible change.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the salt that dissolved is got back (unchanged) / no new substance was made / the salt can be separated out again by evaporating the water.
questions.e: The salt that dissolved in the sea water is **got back again, unchanged**, when the water evaporates. No new substance was made, so dissolving is a reversible (physical) change.
questions.p:
Question 7
Near the Red Sea coast there are salt pans. Sea water is let into wide, shallow pools. Over several weeks the water evaporates in the sunshine and salt is left behind.

questions.q: (b) Which statement describes the evaporation in the salt pans?
c: It happens only at the surface of the water, below the boiling point.
It happens only when the water reaches 100 °C.
It makes large bubbles of gas all through the water.
It changes the water into salt.
questions.e: **Evaporation** happens at the **surface** of a liquid at **any temperature below its boiling point** (here, warmed by the Sun). **Boiling** happens at the boiling point, with bubbles of gas forming all through the liquid. Answer A.
questions.p:
Question 7
Near the Red Sea coast there are salt pans. Sea water is let into wide, shallow pools. Over several weeks the water evaporates in the sunshine and salt is left behind.

questions.q: (c) What mass of water evaporated?
questions.e: Mass of water = mass of sea water − mass of salt = 200 − 8 = **192 g**.
questions.p:
Question 7 (continued)
Omar heats 200 g of sea water in a dish until all the water has evaporated. 8 g of salt is left in the dish.

questions.q: (d) Which substance is a solid at 500 °C?
questions.e: At 500 °C: mercury is above its boiling point (357 °C), so it is a gas; water is above 100 °C, so it is a gas; **salt** is below its melting point (801 °C), so it is still a **solid**.
questions.p:
Question 7 (continued)
The table shows the melting points and boiling points of three substances.
Substance | Melting point (°C) | Boiling point (°C)
mercury | −39 | 357
water | 0 | 100
salt | 801 | 1465

questions.q: (e) Omar says: "We can use a boiling point to help identify a pure substance." Why is he right?
c: The boiling point depends on how much liquid there is.
Each pure substance has its own boiling point.
The boiling point changes every day.
questions.e: The temperature at which a substance changes state is a **property of that substance**: each pure substance has its own melting point and boiling point (water 100 °C, mercury 357 °C). It does not depend on the amount. Answer C.

mercury | −39 | 357
water | 0 | 100
salt | 801 | 1465

questions.q: (c) Which material is best for the walls of the cool box?
questions.e: The walls must stop heat getting in, so they should be a **poor thermal conductor (a thermal insulator)**. Plastic foam is a thermal insulator; copper, steel and aluminium are metals and are good thermal conductors. Answer C.
questions.p:
Question 8 (continued)
The family keeps their drinks cold in a cool box on the beach.

questions.q: (a) What type of rock is granite?
questions.e: Granite formed when **magma cooled and solidified**, so it is **igneous** rock (it has large interlocking crystals because it cooled slowly).
questions.p:
Question 9
The mountains near the Red Sea coast contain granite. Granite formed deep underground when magma cooled slowly. Rain, wind and waves break the granite into small grains, which are carried away to the beach and the sea.

questions.q: (b) What is the name of the process in which the granite is worn away and the grains are carried to the sea?
questions.e: **Erosion** — rock is worn away and the pieces are carried away by water, wind or ice. Answer B.
questions.p:
Question 9
The mountains near the Red Sea coast contain granite. Granite formed deep underground when magma cooled slowly. Rain, wind and waves break the granite into small grains, which are carried away to the beach and the sea.

questions.q: (c) The grains settle on the sea floor. Describe how they could become sedimentary rock, and then later become metamorphic rock.
questions.ms: 1 mark: layers of grains/sediment build up (sedimentation) and are buried, squeezed/compacted (and cemented) into sedimentary rock (e.g. sandstone). 1 mark: the sedimentary rock is buried deeper and is heated and squeezed (high temperature and pressure) WITHOUT melting, which changes it into metamorphic rock. Do not accept: 'it melts' for the second mark.
questions.e:
1. The grains settle in **layers** (sedimentation). More layers on top **bury** them, and the weight **squeezes** them and sticks them together into **sedimentary rock** such as sandstone.
2. If this rock is **buried deeper**, great **heat and pressure** change it — without melting it — into **metamorphic rock** (sandstone becomes quartzite).
questions.p:
Question 9
The mountains near the Red Sea coast contain granite. Granite formed deep underground when magma cooled slowly. Rain, wind and waves break the granite into small grains, which are carried away to the beach and the sea.

questions.q: (a) Omar sees the full moon on 1 June. About when will he next see a full moon?
questions.e: The Moon takes about **one month (about 29½ days)** to go through all its phases, so the next full moon is about 1 July. (On about 15 June it would be a new moon.) Answer D.
questions.p:
Question 10
At night on the beach, Omar sees a full moon.

questions.q: (b) Omar's sister says: "The Moon changes shape during the month because the Earth's shadow covers part of it." Explain the real reason the Moon's shape seems to change.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the Moon orbits the Earth, so we see different amounts of the half of the Moon that is lit by the Sun (accept: we see different parts of its sunlit side as it moves round the Earth). Do not accept: 'the Moon changes shape' / 'clouds cover it'.
questions.e: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon **orbits the Earth**, we see **different amounts of its sunlit half** from the Earth, so its shape seems to change. The Earth's shadow is not the cause.
questions.p:

questions.q: (c) Which list shows these planets in order of distance from the Sun, starting with the closest?
questions.e: The order of the planets from the Sun is Mercury, **Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter**, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Answer A.

blocks.title: After the test
items: **Check every wrong answer.** Read the worked solution, then cover it and do the question again on paper until you can explain it yourself.
**Mark your written answers strictly.** A mark is given only for a point that matches the mark scheme. Two points are needed for 2 marks.
**Sort your mistakes:** was it a fact you did not know, a misread question, a missing unit, or a graph/table you read wrongly? Exam technique mistakes are the quickest to fix.

**Revisit the lessons:** food webs and toxins → *Food Chains, Food Webs, Energy and Toxins*; heart, blood vessels and lungs → *The Heart and Circulatory System* and *The Lungs and Respiratory System*; disease and hygiene → *Diseases, Hygiene and the Body's Defences*; puberty → *Human Reproductive System and Puberty*.

Chemistry → *Properties of Substances: Melting and Boiling Points, Gases, Conductors*, *Reversible Changes and Dissolving*, *Boiling and Evaporation*, *Chemical Reactions: Reactants, Products and Evidence*.
Physics → *Mass, Weight and Gravity*, *Force Diagrams and Forces on Moving Objects*, *Floating and Sinking*, *Light: Reflection and Refraction*, *Electric Circuits, Symbols, Series and Parallel*.

Earth and space → *Rocks and Fossils*, *Types of Soil*, *The Rock Cycle*, *The Solar System and the Phases of the Moon*. Investigation questions (variables, anomalous results, means, conclusions, improving a method) → *Thinking and Working Scientifically: Investigations, Variables, Tables and Graphs*.
When you are ready, try **Practice Test 2** under timed conditions and compare your scores.
